---
title: "Class 7. Split, apply, combine (solutions)"
format: html
---

**Question for today:** Which penguin species is the heaviest, and how do the groups differ?

```{r}
#| label: setup
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, palmerpenguins, here)
```

## 1. The idea

1. **Split** the rows into groups: `group_by()`.
2. **Apply** a summary to each group: `summarize()`.
3. **Combine** the results in one new table (dplyr does this).

Mean body mass of each species:

```{r}
#| label: idea
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarize(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE))
```

`na.rm = TRUE` ignores missing values. Without it, one `NA` turns the mean into `NA`.

## 2. Several summaries in one table

Each summary has a name on the left of `=` and a function on the right. `n()` counts the rows of the group.

```{r}
#| label: several
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_mass = median(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

Two groups: put two columns in `group_by()`.

```{r}
#| label: two-groups
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  group_by(species, sex) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

**Your turn 1:** Make a table with the number of penguins, the mean flipper length and the median flipper length per island.

```{r}
#| label: turn-1
penguins |>
  group_by(island) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean_flipper = mean(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_flipper = median(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

## 3. count() and arrange()

`count()` is `group_by()` plus `n()` in one step. `arrange(desc())` puts the largest value first.

```{r}
#| label: count
penguins |>
  count(species, island) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

**Your turn 2:** Which species and sex has the highest mean body mass? Use `filter(!is.na(sex))`, `group_by()`, `summarize()` and `arrange(desc())`.

```{r}
#| label: turn-2
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  group_by(species, sex) |>
  summarize(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(mean_mass))
```

Answer: male Gentoo penguins (about 5,485 g).

## 4. A sorted bar chart of group means

The summary table goes straight into `ggplot()`. The table already holds the values, so we use `geom_col()`. `fct_reorder()` sorts the bars by the mean.

```{r}
#| label: bar
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarize(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_mass, y = fct_reorder(species, mean_mass))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Mean body mass (g)", y = NULL)
```

**Your turn 3:** Draw the same chart for the mean bill length (`bill_length_mm`).

```{r}
#| label: turn-3
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarize(mean_bill = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_bill, y = fct_reorder(species, mean_bill))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Mean bill length (mm)", y = NULL)
```

## 5. Latvian Labour Force Survey: employed people by sex

Codes: `EKA` = 1 employed, 2 unemployed, 3 inactive. `B11` = 1 male, 2 female (see `data/lfs_codebook.md`).

```{r}
#| label: lfs
here("data", "lfs_2025_example.csv") |>
  read_csv(show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(EKA == 1) |>
  mutate(sex = case_when(B11 == 1 ~ "Male", B11 == 2 ~ "Female")) |>
  count(sex)
```

Check: the sample file holds a few rows. Replace it with the full file under the same name to get real counts.

> Deliverable: one grouped table and one bar chart.
